paper_title: Fast-JEPA: Advancing the Success-Latency Frontier for Latent World Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Latent world models predict the outcomes of action sequences, but comparing candidate plans through recursive rollout remains expensive at test time. We introduce Fast-JEPA, a latent world model planning framework that advances the success-latency Pareto frontier of predictive search. Fast-JEPA reorganizes predictive computation to support effective action-sequence search at low planning cost. It constructs a goal-directed plan to guide search and directly predicts the outcomes of complete candidates for efficient comparison, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, Fast-JEPA achieves 96.50% average success rate with 2.41x faster planning than INTACT. Search-budget sweeps show that its competitive success and low latency extend across candidate counts and refinement depths. We further introduce DynaGoal, a benchmark for evaluating world-model planning under dynamic out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines, and controlled response delays. Fast-JEPA achieves average success rates of 73.83% on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoal-Deadline, demonstrating the practical value of low-latency predictive planning under changing control conditions and execution-time constraints. Our project page is available at https://deepcybo-physai.github.io/Fast-JEPA.

sections.content: Latent world models predict the outcomes of action sequences, but comparing candidate plans through recursive rollout remains expensive at test time. We introduce Fast-JEPA, latent world model planning framework that advances the successlatency Pareto frontier of predictive search. Fast-JEPA reorganizes predictive computation to support effective action-sequence search at low planning cost. It constructs goal-directed plan to guide search and directly predicts the outcomes of complete candidates for efficient comparison, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, Fast-JEPA achieves 96.50% average success rate with 2.41 faster planning than INTACT. Search-budget sweeps show that its competitive success and low latency extend across candidate counts and refinement depths. We further introduce DynaGoal, benchmark for evaluating world-model planning under dynamic out-ofdistribution conditions, execution deadlines, and controlled response delays. Fast-JEPA achieves average success rates of 73.83% on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoalDeadline, demonstrating the practical value of low-latency predictive planning under changing control conditions and execution-time constraints. Our project page is available at https://deepcybo-physai.github.io/Fast-JEPA/. 1. Introduction World models enable visual controllers to compare action sequences through predicted outcomes in representation space [15, 24]. However, evaluating many candidate sequences through predictive search can incur substantial online computation. This raises central question: how can world-model planning advance the successlatency Pareto Corresponding author. Work done during internship at DeepCybo. Figure 1. Advancing the successlatency Pareto frontier. FastJEPA achieves 96.50% average success rate at 10.88 ms, improving the observed frontier among the locally evaluated configurations and running 2.41 faster than INTACT. frontier while retaining the benefits of predictive search? complete planner must decide both which actions are worth considering and how much computation to spend comparing them. strong initial plan reduces the burden on search, but it does not eliminate the potential value of comparing alternatives. Under limited online budget, refinement must explore useful candidates while controlling the cost of their evaluation. With recursive scoring, each candidate requires chain of intermediate state predictions, and this computation is repeated across search rounds. Action construction and candidate comparison expose different information to the planner. During sequential construction, later actions remain unspecified, so intermediate outcome predictions provide context for subsequent action choices. Once candidate is complete, all its actions are known. Under terminal visual-goal objective, comparison requires only its predicted endpoint. This distinction motivates retaining intermediate queries for action construction and using direct terminal queries for candidate evaluation. 1 We introduce Fast-JEPA, planning framework that reorganizes predictive computation to support actionsequence search at low planning cost (Figure 2). FastJEPA constructs goal-directed plan through world-modelguided action generation, providing starting point for predictive search. Complete candidate sequences are then compared through direct terminal predictions under shared visual-goal objective, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. By concentrating search around an informed plan while reducing repeated candidate-evaluation costs, Fast-JEPA retains the benefits of predictive search within substantially lower computational budget. To evaluate world-model planning under dynamic outof-distribution (OOD) conditions and temporal constraints, we introduce DynaGoal, benchmark comprising three complementary protocols across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom. DynaGoal-Shift evaluates adaptation to changing goals and environment geometry, while DynaGoalDeadline measures goal completion under joint planning and execution time budgets. DynaGoal-Delay further examines robustness to controlled response delays as environments evolve between observation and action. Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, FastJEPA achieves 96.50% average success rate with mean complete planning latency of 10.88 ms. This search-based controller plans 2.41 faster than INTACT while attaining higher average success (Figure 1). Search-budget sweeps show that its low-latency operating region extends across candidate counts and refinement depths, and the scoring comparison links lower planning cost to cheaper candidate evaluation. Fast-JEPA also achieves 73.83% average success on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoalDeadline. Together, these results demonstrate that FastJEPA maintains competitive success at substantially lower planning latency. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: We present Fast-JEPA, world-model planning framework that advances the successlatency Pareto frontier by reorganizing predictive computation for efficient actionsequence search. We introduce DynaGoal, benchmark evaluating worldmodel planning under out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines, and response delays. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Fast-JEPA advances the successlatency Pareto frontier of worldmodel planning across diverse control tasks. 2. Related Work Latent world models. Visual foresight and latent dynamics enable action selection through predicted outcomes [8, 10, 15]. Dreamer learns behavior through imagined trajectories [16, 17], while TD-MPC couples latent planning with learned policies and value estimates [18, 19]. Predictive representation learning extends this direction from images to video [2, 3, 5]. LeWM learns visual latent dynamics [24], while Fast-LeWM improves prediction efficiency through structural design [13]. FIRM-WM studies state-factorized recurrent dynamics for visual planning, while RC-aux introduces multi-horizon prediction and reachability supervision [22, 36]. Together, these works develop predictive representations and dynamics for control through different temporal prediction structures. Goal-directed action learning and planning. Goalconditioned learning supplies policies for reaching desired states [1, 14, 25]. Action-chunk and diffusion policies generate candidate behavior through sequence modeling [7, 21, 39]. GC-IDM amortizes control into inverse dynamics [26], while INTACT studies intent-to-action learning and reference-guided search for latent control [32]. Learned priors guide planning in POPLIN [35], and samplingbased improvements such as iCEM improve search efficiency [30]. LeFlow generates latent paths and verifies their decoded actions, while LEAP refines goal-conditioned proposals through differentiable rollouts [20, 29]. IMWM combines retrieval initialization with hybrid scoring [12], whereas NGC uses neighborhood graphs to define latentspace goal distances [37]. Together, these approaches illustrate different ways to guide candidate generation, evaluation, and selection in predictive control. 3. Fast-JEPA Fast-JEPA organizes world-model queries according to the information required during search (Figure 2). During action construction, outcomes predicted from the observed anchor under the selected actions inform subsequent action choices. Once an action sequence is complete, its predicted terminal outcome is sufficient for comparison under the visual-goal objective. The framework retains sequential dependence in action construction while avoiding recursive state prediction during candidate evaluation. 3.1. All tasks reuse models trained on the original environments without additional training or fine-tuning. DynaGoal-Shift. These tasks introduce changing targets or environment geometry during control. PushT uses drifting target that reverses direction. Reacher and Cube switch targets, and TwoRoom contains continuously moving doorway (Figure 3(a)). Success requires sustained goal reaching for PushT and TwoRoom, and completion before and after the target change for Reacher and Cube. Measured planning delay determines when new plan becomes available, directly connecting planning cost to control performance in continuously evolving environments. DynaGoal-Deadline. These tasks require goal completion within task-specific deadlines that account for both cumulative planning time and action execution duration. Success therefore depends on the planners ability to complete the task within the strict time budget by balancing planning and execution time. Appendix B.2 specifies the Shift and Deadline task conditions, success criteria, and timing rules. DynaGoal-Delay. These evaluations extend the four Shift tasks with controlled total response delays of 0, 300, 500, and 800 ms. They assess robustness as the interval between observation and plan execution increases (Figure 3(b,c)). During this interval, the environment advances using buffered actions from the previous plan, holding the last action when the buffer is empty. The new plan replaces the remaining buffered actions once available. The imposed delay sets the response interval independently of measured planning time. Each controller is evaluated on 100 episodes per task at each delay level using the Shift success criteria. 5. Experiments We evaluate whether predictive search can deliver competitive control at low planning latency. Complete-controller comparisons establish the successlatency operating point, DynaGoal tests performance under changing and timeconstrained control conditions, and targeted component analyses examine the search starting point and candidateevaluation cost. Search-budget sweeps and qualitative behavioral examples assess how these choices affect the available operating points and selected actions. Evaluation setting. We evaluate PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom using the standard native startgoal and success conventions of the latent-control benchmarks [13, 24, 32]. The main comparisons average 100 episodes per task over three independently trained models. We report success rate and warmed batch-one complete planning latency on an RTX PRO 6000 GPU. DynaGoal reuses the original-task models without fine-tuning. Full task, implementation, and detailed timing protocols appear in Appendix B. 5.1. Main Results on Four Tasks Fast-JEPA performs predictive search at lower completeplanning latency than INTACT while achieving the highest average success among the locally evaluated methods  (Table 1)  . It reaches 96.50% at 10.88 ms, compared with 95.58% at 26.19 ms for INTACT. This corresponds to 2.41 speedup with higher average success rate. Relative to INTACT Guarded A, Fast-JEPA maintains similar success level while reducing planning time from 127.09 to 10.88 ms. This operating point demonstrates that retaining candidate search is compatible with low-latency control.

Ablation Studies Proposal focuses search. Removing the proposal lowers average success from 96.33% to 68.17% at the same search budget  (Table 4)  . Candidate evaluation alone is therefore insufficient to recover the complete controllers performance from broad initialization. The proposal supplies productive neighborhood and retained plan, allowing refinement to focus on plausible alternatives. Effective search thus depends not only on how many candidates are evaluated, but also on where that evaluation is concentrated. Refinement beyond the proposal. Without refinement, the controller achieves 93.83% success at 5.53 ms, while full Fast-JEPA reaches 96.33% at 10.78 ms. The gains are task-dependent: refinement improves PushT and Reacher, while Cube already achieves 100% success without refinement. This suggests that additional search is most valuable when the initial proposal leaves room for improvement. Proposal-only execution remains useful low-cost mode, while refinement provides an opportunity to improve control through candidate comparison. 5.4. Across candidate counts and refinement depths, Fast-JEPA achieves competitive success within substantially lower latency range. 5.5. Alternative planning designs. Table 5 compares alternative proposal and scoring designs under matched search budgets. Replacing predictionguided construction with GC-IDM proposal reduces average success from 96.33% to 94.42% and increases planning latency to 132.91 ms. An oracle-state proposal achieves comparable success (95.77%) but requires 781.34 ms due to simulator rollouts, supporting the efficiency of learned intermediate predictions. For candidate evaluation, direct terminal scoring achieves 96.33% success at 10.78 ms, compared with 96.08% at 20.54 ms for recursive scoring, reducing scoring time from 11.16 to 2.32 ms. These comparisons reveal an asymmetry in the role of prediction during planning. Intermediate predictions help construct useful action sequences, whereas recursively predicting intermediate states during candidate evaluation provides little additional benefit under the terminal-goal objective. The consistent advantage of direct scoring across proposals supports allocating predictive computation according to the information required at each planning stage. Table 6 reports training costs across tasks. Fast-JEPA requires 5.95 GPU-hours, compared with 6.67 for INTACT, 18.16 for LeWM, and 188.05 for Fast-LeWM. Its lowlatency planning does not incur additional training costs. 5.6. Qualitative Refinement Behavior The examples in Figure 6 show refinement changing the final control outcome. In PushT, the refined trajectory reaches the success criterion while the proposal-only trajectory remains unsuccessful within the evaluation budget. In Cube, the proposal-only trajectory drops the object onto the table, whereas Fast-JEPA retains the grasp and reaches the goal. These cases illustrate how candidate comparison can produce useful behavioral corrections after an informed initial proposal. The paired runs share initial states and goals, and Appendix records their evaluation interpretation. 6. Conclusion We presented Fast-JEPA, world-model framework that advances the successlatency Pareto frontier through efficient 8 predictive computation. Intermediate predictions guide action construction, while direct terminal queries evaluate plans without recursive rollout. Fast-JEPA achieves 96.50% average success at 10.88 ms across four tasks. Searchbudget sweeps confirm its efficiency across configurations, while DynaGoal evaluates out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines, and response delays.
